1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5.name: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5.background: Carl Jaenisch originated it and analysed it in the December 1847 issue of Le Palamède. It was named after the German lawyer Adolph Schliemann in the Handbuch des Schachspiels, although the line Schliemann himself advocated in the 1860s was a gambit with ...Bc5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Nc3.strategy: Guards e4 and develops, the more aggressive way to meet the f-pawn thrust: recapturing with the knight puts a piece in the centre. The price is theory, since White must know sharp lines to turn the position into an advantage.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Nc3.name: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defence, Dyckhoff Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Nc3.background: With 4.d3, this is the most common reply to 3...f5, although 4.d3 has surpassed it in popularity in recent years.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Bxc6.strategy: Gives up the bishop pair to remove the knight, hoping to win e5, but ...dxc6 opens the queen's diagonal: ...Qd4 forks the knight and the e4 pawn and wins the pawn back at once. White has given up the bishop pair for no advantage.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Bxc6.name: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defence, Exchange Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Bxc6.background: Carl Jaenisch analysed this exchange in the December 1847 issue of Le Palamède, together with 4.d4 and 4.exf5. It is rarely seen.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.d4.strategy: Counters on e5 rather than guarding e4. If Black takes on e4, White exchanges on c6 and captures on e5, regaining the pawn with an open game, though this is a less testing choice than simply defending e4.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.d4.name: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defence, Schönemann Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.d4.background: Carl Jaenisch analysed 4.d4 in the December 1847 issue of Le Palamède, together with 4.exf5 and 4.Bxc6.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.exf5.strategy: Takes the pawn, but ...e4 hits the knight, which has no comfortable square: e5 and d4 are covered by the c6 knight, g5 and h4 by the queen. White is driven back, and Black gets the better game despite the pawn.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.exf5.name: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defence, Jaenisch Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.exf5.background: Carl Jaenisch analysed this capture in the December 1847 issue of Le Palamède, together with 4.d4 and 4.Bxc6.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Nc3 fxe4.strategy: The only consistent move: the f-pawn attacked e4, and anything else gives White the centre for nothing. Black opens the f-file and removes White's central pawn, at the price of a weak pawn on e5 that only the c6 knight defends.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Nc3 fxe4 5..strategy: Recaptures with the knight, which sits strongly on e4 and eyes d6 and f6. White keeps a lead in development, and Black must choose how to challenge the knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Nc3 fxe4 5..name: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defence, Tartakower Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Nc3 fxe4 5..background: 5...Nf6 has increased in popularity to the point that it is now often considered the main line after 4.Nc3. Teimour Radjabov, who plays the gambit regularly, prefers it.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Nc3 fxe4 5..strategy: Challenges the knight with a developing move and avoids the forcing lines of the pawn thrust. Black plays for activity and the bishop pair, usually at the cost of the e5 pawn; it is now often considered the main line.

Challenges the knight with a pawn and builds a classical centre, leading to well-analysed lines of the gambit. A retreat by the knight would leave Black doing well, but White has a sharp sacrifice in reply, and Black has scored poorly in those lines.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Nc3 fxe4 5..name: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defence, Kostić Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Nc3 fxe4 5..strategy: A quiet developing move that prepares to castle but does not challenge the strong knight on e4, and e5 depends on the c6 knight alone. It avoids the sharp pawn lines, yet Black has given White a free hand.

The critical answer to the pawn push: White takes e5 and lets Black win the knight on e4, banking on the attack against Black's uncastled king that follows. The lines are long and forcing, and Black has scored badly in them.

Takes the knight on e4 and is a piece up for a moment, but White's Nxc6 answers with a tempo on the queen, so Black must play accurately to keep an uncastled king safe. Declining leaves White a pawn up.
